props.explanation: Aggregating a period's orders into one crossing dampens the volatility that continuous matching produces at those moments, which is why many equity markets set official opening and closing prices this way. The batch is also where the day's largest concentrations of interest meet.

atoms.title: continuous trading discovery
atoms.summary: Price discovery tick by tick, as individual orders match through the session.

props.source_wording: Prices update tick-by-tick as orders match Provides real-time price information Can be noisy in thin markets
props.explanation: It gives a live price at every moment, which is its value, and it is noisy in thin markets, which is its cost -- a single small order can move the print. It is the mode in which most of the session runs, bracketed by [[Auction-Based Discovery]] at each end.

atoms.title: cross-market discovery
atoms.summary: Price discovery that happens between related instruments rather than within one book.

props.source_wording: Futures often lead spot price discovery Options markets embed volatility expectations ADRs and local shares influence each other ETFs and underlying baskets arbitrage to equilibrium
props.explanation: Futures often lead spot, options embed a volatility expectation the underlying does not show, and ETFs and their baskets are pulled together by arbitrage. The consequence is that the price of one instrument carries information about another before that other has moved, which is what lead-lag analysis looks for and what [[Arbitrageurs]] enforce.

atoms.title: information share (hasbrouck)
atoms.summary: The quantity information share (hasbrouck).

props.formula: Information Share = Var(market_i contribution to efficient price) / Var(total efficient price)

variance_contribution.description: variance of this market's contribution to the efficient price

variance_total.description: variance of the total efficient price

atoms.title: component share
atoms.summary: The quantity component share.

props.formula: Component Share = Var(permanent price impact from market_i) / Var(total permanent price impact)

permanent_impact_market.description: permanent price impact from this market

atoms.title: price efficiency ratio
atoms.summary: The quantity price efficiency ratio.

props.formula: Efficiency = Variance(Returns over long horizon) / (n * Variance(Returns over short horizon))

var_long.description: return variance over the long horizon

var_short.description: return variance over the short horizon

atoms.title: core principles
atoms.summary: Things that are true of this market whether or not anyone acts on them. A strategy does not get to disagree with one: it either accounts for it or pays for it.

principles: Temporary vs. Permanent Impact: Some price impact reverses (temporary), some persists (permanent/information)

atoms.title: best practices
atoms.summary: Things we follow because someone has already paid to learn them. Each is a default rather than a rule -- departing from one is often right, but it should be a decision with a reason.

practices: Be aware of the potential impact of large orders on market prices and plan execution accordingly
Study the specific microstructure characteristics of each market traded (e.g., tick sizes, trading hours, circuit breakers)
Account for all transaction costs when calculating expected strategy returns
Trade when your counterparty is likely to be uninformed (e.g., index rebalancing flows)
Avoid trading patterns that reveal your strategy to sophisticated participants
Break large orders into smaller child orders to reduce footprint
Avoid trading during illiquid periods (market open, lunch hour, holidays)
Monitor real-time market depth before executing larger orders
Use regime detection filters to enable/disable specific strategies
Adapt trading strategies to current market conditions rather than forcing one approach
Backtest strategies across multiple regimes to understand performance variation
Have predefined plans for regime transitions rather than reacting emotionally
Select venues based on order characteristics (size, urgency, information sensitivity)
Monitor execution quality metrics across venues
Understand fee structures (maker-taker rebates can influence routing)
Factor spread costs into strategy profitability calculations
Monitor spread changes as an indicator of market conditions
Monitor lead-lag relationships between related markets
Use pre-market and after-hours trading for early information
Understand the price discovery role of derivatives markets
Be cautious trading immediately after major information releases
Recognize that the first price after news is often not the right price

atoms.title: spot markets
atoms.summary: A market where an instrument is bought and sold for immediate delivery at the current price.

applications: Long-term investment and portfolio construction
Basis for derivatives pricing (spot-futures relationships)
Arbitrage between spot and derivative markets
Direct exposure to asset price movements
Dividend capture and income strategies
props.source_wording: Spot markets (also called cash markets) are financial markets where financial instruments are traded for immediate delivery and settlement. The "spot price" represents the current market price at which an asset can be bought or sold for immediate exchange.
props.explanation: What is traded is the asset itself rather than a claim on it later, so there is no expiration to manage and the holder has the full rights of ownership. The spot price is the reference every derivative is priced against, through the [[Cost of Carry Relationship]].

atoms.title: equity spot market
atoms.summary: The market for immediate purchase of shares, conveying ownership of the company.

examples: Purchase 100 shares of AAPL at $175.50 Settlement: T+2 (trade date plus two business days) Ownership: Full shareholder rights, dividends, voting
props.explanation: The buyer receives the full rights of a shareholder -- dividends, votes, corporate actions -- which is the difference between holding stock and holding a derivative on it. Settlement takes two business days.

atoms.title: forex spot market
atoms.summary: The market for immediate exchange of one currency for another at the prevailing rate.

examples: Buy EUR/USD at 1.0850 Settlement: T+2 (standard for major pairs) Delivery: Exchange of currency amounts
props.explanation: Every price is a ratio of two currencies rather than the price of a thing, so a position is always long one and short the other. Major pairs settle two business days out, and holding past the close pays or receives the interest differential between them.

atoms.title: cryptocurrency spot market
atoms.summary: The market for immediate purchase of a cryptocurrency, settling on the blockchain or within an exchange ledger.

examples: Buy 1 BTC at $45,000 Settlement: Near-instantaneous (blockchain confirmation) Custody: Direct ownership, can withdraw to personal wallet
props.explanation: Settlement is close to immediate and the asset can be withdrawn to a wallet the holder controls, which is the feature the asset class is built around. Trading runs continuously, so a position is exposed at every hour rather than only during a session.

atoms.title: commodity spot market
atoms.summary: The market for immediate purchase of a physical commodity, at the price for prompt delivery.

examples: Buy 100 oz gold at $1,950/oz Settlement: Varies (T+2 or physical delivery arrangements) Delivery: Can take physical delivery or hold in vault
props.explanation: Ownership here is of a physical thing, so the cost of holding it -- storage, insurance, financing -- is real and shows up in the [[Cost of Carry Relationship]] between spot and futures. Settlement conventions vary with the commodity, and delivery can be taken or the position held in a vault.

atoms.title: spot return
atoms.summary: The change in price over a period, as a simple percentage or as a log return.

props.formula:
Simple Return = (P_t - P_(t-1)) / P_(t-1)
Log Return = ln(P_t / P_(t-1))
props.source_wording: The quantity spot return.
props.explanation: The two are not interchangeable: simple returns aggregate across positions in a portfolio, log returns aggregate across time and are what volatility and most models are computed on.

atoms.title: total return (with dividends)
atoms.summary: The return of a holding including the income it pays, not only its change in price.

props.formula: Total Return = (P_t - P_(t-1) + Dividends) / P_(t-1)
props.source_wording: The quantity total return (with dividends).
props.explanation: Price return understates what a dividend-paying holding earned and misstates any comparison against an instrument that pays nothing; it is also the yield term that shows up in the [[Cost of Carry Relationship]].

atoms.title: cost of carry relationship
atoms.summary: The fair price of a forward or future is the spot price carried forward at the financing rate net of any yield the asset pays.

props.formula: Futures Price = Spot Price * e^((r - y) * T)
props.source_wording: The identity cost of carry relationship.
props.explanation: It is an arbitrage identity rather than a forecast: if the future strays from it, the trade is to buy one leg, sell the other and hold to expiration. It explains contango and backwardation as facts about rates, storage and convenience yield rather than as opinions about direction, and it is the same identity §2.2 restates as F = S * e^((r - y) * T).

atoms.title: futures
atoms.summary: A standardised contract to buy or sell an asset at an agreed price on a stated future date.

applications: Hedging existing spot positions against price risk
Speculating on price direction with leverage
Calendar spreads (trading the difference between expiration months)
Basis trading (spot-futures arbitrage)
Rolling exposure without physical delivery
examples: Futures Contract: Asset: E-mini S&P 500 (ES) Contract Size: $50 x S&P 500 Index Tick Size: 0.25 points ($12.50) Expiration: Quarterly (March, June, September, December) Settlement: Cash settled to index value

Contango vs. Backwardation: **Contango**: Futures price > Spot price (normal for storable commodities) **Backwardation**: Futures price < Spot price (indicates supply shortage or high convenience yield)

Perpetual Swap Funding: BTC-PERP trading at $45,100 (spot at $45,000) Premium indicates more longs than shorts Funding rate: +0.01% every 8 hours Longs pay shorts to hold positions Incentivizes arbitrage to close premium
props.source_wording: Standardized contracts obligating the buyer to purchase, or the seller to sell, an asset at a predetermined price on a specified future date.
props.explanation: The obligation is symmetric -- unlike an [[Option]], both sides must perform -- and the position is marked to market daily, so profit and loss are paid as they accrue rather than at expiration. Because only margin is posted, a small deposit controls a large notional, and the price converges on spot as expiration approaches.

atoms.title: perpetual swaps
atoms.summary: A futures-like contract with no expiration, held to the spot price by a periodic funding payment between longs and shorts.

props.source_wording: Derivative contracts similar to futures but with no expiration date, commonly used in cryptocurrency markets, with periodic funding rate payments to maintain price alignment with spot.
props.explanation: Without an expiration there is no convergence to enforce the price, so funding does it: when the contract trades above spot, longs pay shorts and the premium is arbitraged away. It is the dominant crypto derivative, and the funding rate is a running cost or income on a position rather than a detail of it.

atoms.title: basis
atoms.summary: The difference between the futures price and the spot price, in price terms or as a percentage of spot.

props.formula:
Basis = Futures Price - Spot Price
Basis (%) = (F - S) / S * 100%
props.source_wording: The quantity basis.
props.explanation: It carries the market's financing and storage costs and converges to zero at expiration, which is what makes it tradeable in its own right. Positive is contango, negative is backwardation, and the sign is information about supply rather than about direction.

atoms.title: annualized basis
atoms.summary: The basis expressed as an annual rate, scaled by the days remaining to expiration.

props.formula: Annualized Basis = (F/S - 1) * (365 / Days to Expiry) * 100%
props.source_wording: The quantity annualized basis.
props.explanation: It is what makes two contracts with different expirations comparable, and it turns the basis into the yield of a cash-and-carry trade: buy spot, sell the future, and collect it to expiration.

atoms.title: perpetual funding rate
atoms.summary: The periodic payment between longs and shorts on a perpetual contract, proportional to position value.

props.formula: Funding Payment = Position Value * Funding Rate
props.source_wording: The quantity perpetual funding rate.
props.explanation: It is the mechanism that substitutes for expiration: a positive rate means the contract is above spot and longs pay to hold, which draws in the arbitrage that closes the premium. As a running cost it can exceed the move being traded, and as a signal it says which side is crowded.

atoms.title: contract value
atoms.summary: The value a contract controls: multiplier times price times the number of contracts.

props.formula: Notional Value = Contract Multiplier * Current Price * Number of Contracts
props.source_wording: The quantity contract value.
props.explanation: It is the exposure, as distinct from the margin posted against it, and the two are confused at the trader's expense -- risk is a share of notional while capital is a share of margin. Every position calculation starts here.

atoms.title: options
atoms.summary: A contract conveying the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying at a stated strike price by a stated expiration.

applications: Hedging portfolio against downside risk (protective puts)
Generating income from existing positions (covered calls)
Speculating on direction with defined risk
Volatility trading (straddles, strangles)
Complex multi-leg strategies for specific market views
examples: Covered Call: Own 100 shares AAPL at $175 Sell 1 Call, Strike $185, Premium $2.50 Outcome if price stays below $185: Keep shares + $250 premium Outcome if price exceeds $185: Shares called away at $185, total gain $12.50/share
props.source_wording: Options are derivative contracts that give the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) an underlying asset at a specified price (strike) before or on a specified date (expiration).
props.explanation: The asymmetry is the point: the buyer can lose only the premium while the payoff above the strike is open-ended, which makes an option the instrument for a view with a defined worst case. That optionality is paid for in time value, which decays every day and vanishes at expiration, and is priced from volatility rather than from direction.

atoms.title: call option
atoms.summary: The right, not the obligation, to buy the underlying at the strike price on or before expiration.

examples: AAPL Call, Strike $180, Expiration 30 days Premium: $3.50 Breakeven: $183.50 ($180 + $3.50) Max Loss: $3.50 (premium paid) Max Gain: Unlimited (above breakeven)
props.explanation: The buyer risks only the premium and keeps everything above the strike, which is the asymmetry that makes an option a defined-risk way to hold a directional view. The seller has the mirror image: the premium is the most that can be made and the loss above the strike is unbounded unless the underlying is already held.

atoms.title: put option
atoms.summary: The right, not the obligation, to sell the underlying at the strike price on or before expiration.

examples: SPY Put, Strike $440, Expiration 45 days Premium: $5.00 Breakeven: $435.00 ($440 - $5.00) Max Loss: $5.00 (premium paid) Max Gain: $435.00 (if underlying goes to zero)
props.explanation: It pays as the underlying falls, bounded by a price of zero, which makes it the direct way to insure a holding: the premium is the cost of the insurance and the strike is the level insured. The seller is paid that premium to stand ready to buy at the strike.

atoms.title: black-scholes call price
atoms.summary: Prices a European call from the spot price, strike, time to expiration, interest rate and volatility.

props.formula:
C = S * N(d1) - K * e^(-rT) * N(d2)

d1 = (ln(S/K) + (r + sigma^2/2) * T) / (sigma * sqrt(T))
d2 = d1 - sigma * sqrt(T)
props.source_wording: Computes black-scholes call price.
props.explanation: Every input but one is observable, which is what makes the model useful in reverse: quoted against a market price it returns implied volatility, the number options actually trade on. Its assumptions -- constant volatility, continuous hedging, no jumps -- are why the surface is not flat in practice.

atoms.title: put-call parity
atoms.summary: The identity linking a call and a put at the same strike and expiration to the underlying and a discounted bond.

props.formula: C - P = S - K * e^(-rT)
props.source_wording: The identity put-call parity.
props.explanation: It holds by arbitrage, so it fixes each of the four prices in terms of the other three: an option can be replicated synthetically, and a violation is a riskless trade rather than a view. It is also the check that an implied volatility surface is internally consistent.

atoms.title: the greeks
atoms.summary: The family of sensitivities of an option price: to the underlying, to the rate of that sensitivity, to time, to volatility and to interest rates.

props.formula:
Delta = dV/dS (sensitivity to underlying price)
Gamma = d(Delta)/dS (rate of change of delta)
Theta = dV/dT (time decay per day)
Vega = dV/d(sigma) (sensitivity to volatility)
Rho = dV/dr (sensitivity to interest rates)
props.source_wording: The family the greeks.
props.explanation: Together they say how a position will behave when something changes, which is the whole of options risk management: delta is directional exposure, gamma how fast it moves, theta the daily cost of holding, vega exposure to a change in implied volatility, and rho to rates. They are the reason an option position cannot be managed by direction alone.

atoms.title: intrinsic and time value
atoms.summary: The split of an option premium into what it would be worth if exercised now and what is paid for the time remaining.

props.formula:
Call Intrinsic = max(S - K, 0)
Put Intrinsic = max(K - S, 0)
Time Value = Option Price - Intrinsic Value
props.source_wording: The quantity intrinsic and time value.
props.explanation: Intrinsic value is arithmetic on the strike and the spot price; everything above it is the market's price for uncertainty, and it decays to nothing by expiration. The split is what separates a directional gain from the cost of waiting for one.

atoms.title: margin
atoms.summary: Collateral posted against a position: an initial amount to open it and a maintenance amount to keep it.

applications: Increasing capital efficiency for qualified strategies
Hedging with reduced capital requirements
Short selling (borrowing assets)
Futures and derivatives trading
Crypto perpetual swap trading
examples: Leverage Calculation: Account Balance: $10,000 Position Size: $50,000 Leverage: 5x ($50,000 / $10,000)
Margin Requirements: Initial Margin: 20% ($10,000 for $50,000 position) Maintenance Margin: 10% ($5,000) Liquidation Trigger: When equity falls below $5,000

Liquidation Scenario: Position: 5x Long BTC at $50,000 (1 BTC exposure, $10,000 margin) Liquidation Price: ~$40,000 (20% drop = 100% of margin) Calculation: Entry - (Margin / Position Size) = $50,000 - $10,000 = $40,000

Cross vs. Isolated Margin: Cross Margin: All account funds available for all positions Isolated Margin: Only allocated margin used for specific position Trade-off: Cross provides more buffer but exposes entire account to any position's loss
props.source_wording: Collateral deposited to cover potential losses, expressed as initial margin (to open) and maintenance margin (to maintain positions)
props.explanation: It is a performance bond rather than a payment, and the gap between the two thresholds is the whole of the buffer -- once equity falls through the maintenance level the [[Liquidation Engine]] acts. Held across the account it cushions more, and exposes more; isolated to one position it caps the loss at that position.

atoms.title: leverage
atoms.summary: The ratio of position size to the capital backing it.

props.source_wording: The ratio of position size to margin, amplifying both gains and losses
props.explanation: It amplifies the return on capital in both directions by the same factor, which is why the move that liquidates a position gets smaller as leverage rises: at five times, a twenty per cent adverse move is the whole margin. What it buys is capital efficiency, not edge.

atoms.title: liquidation engine
atoms.summary: The exchange system that closes a position automatically once its margin falls below the maintenance requirement.

props.source_wording: Automated system that forcibly closes positions when margin falls below maintenance requirements
props.explanation: It exists to stop an account going negative and taking the venue with it, so it acts on the exchange's schedule rather than the trader's: the position is closed at whatever the book offers, in the conditions that caused the shortfall. A stop placed above the liquidation price is the trader keeping that decision.

atoms.title: leverage ratio
atoms.summary: Position size divided by the capital backing it; effective leverage compares notional exposure with account equity.

props.formula:
Leverage = Position Size / Margin
Effective Leverage = Notional Exposure / Account Equity
props.source_wording: The quantity leverage ratio.
props.explanation: The two differ once there is more than one position or unrealised profit and loss, and the effective figure is the one that governs risk. It is the multiplier on both return and loss, and it sets how far price can move before the margin is gone.

atoms.title: long position liquidation price
atoms.summary: The price at which a long position's equity falls to the maintenance requirement and it is closed automatically.

props.formula: Liquidation Price = Entry Price * (1 - Initial Margin % + Maintenance Margin %)
props.source_wording: The quantity long position liquidation price.
props.explanation: It follows from entry price and the two margin percentages, so it is knowable before the position is opened -- which is what makes it the first calculation rather than a surprise. Fees and funding move it closer over time.

atoms.title: short position liquidation price
atoms.summary: The price at which a short position's equity falls to the maintenance requirement and it is closed automatically.

props.formula: Liquidation Price = Entry Price * (1 + Initial Margin % - Maintenance Margin %)
props.source_wording: The quantity short position liquidation price.
props.explanation: The arithmetic mirrors the long case, but the exposure does not: a short loses as price rises, and price can rise without bound, so the distance to liquidation is the whole of the protection.

atoms.title: margin ratio
atoms.summary: Maintenance margin required as a share of account equity.

props.formula: Margin Ratio = Maintenance Margin Required / Account Equity
props.source_wording: The quantity margin ratio.
props.explanation: It is the single number that says how close a position is to being closed out: at a hundred per cent the [[Liquidation Engine]] acts. Watching it is how leverage is managed in practice, because it moves with price, with funding and with the margin the venue demands in volatility.

atoms.title: return amplification
atoms.summary: The return on capital under leverage: the underlying return multiplied by the leverage used.

props.formula:
Leveraged Return = Leverage * Underlying Return
5x leverage, 2% move = 10% return (or loss)
props.source_wording: The quantity return amplification.
props.explanation: It is symmetric, which is the part that gets forgotten -- five times leverage turns a two per cent move into ten per cent in whichever direction it goes, and a twenty per cent adverse move into the whole account.

atoms.title: crypto-specific mechanics
atoms.summary: The trading infrastructure particular to digital assets: continuous markets, self-custody, on-chain settlement and pool-based venues.

applications: Trading on centralized exchanges (CEX) for liquidity and speed
Decentralized exchange (DEX) trading for self-custody and permissionless access
Yield farming and liquidity provision on AMMs
Cross-chain arbitrage
On-chain derivatives trading
props.source_wording: Crypto-specific mechanics encompass the unique trading infrastructure, settlement systems, and market structures particular to cryptocurrency and digital asset markets, including decentralized exchanges, automated market makers, and blockchain-based settlement.
props.explanation: What sets the asset class apart is not the price behaviour but the plumbing. Markets never close, so there is no opening auction and no overnight gap; assets can be held directly, so counterparty risk is a choice; and settlement is a blockchain fact with a fee and a confirmation time attached.

atoms.title: centralized exchange (cex)
atoms.summary: A crypto venue that holds customer assets and matches orders on its own book, off chain.

props.source_wording: Examples: Binance, Coinbase, Kraken Order book model, high liquidity Custody held by exchange KYC required, faster execution Counterparty risk to exchange
props.explanation: It offers the deepest liquidity and the fastest matching in the asset class, at the cost of custody: the balance is the exchange's promise rather than a key you hold. Access is gated by identity checks, and settlement is an entry in an internal ledger until a withdrawal takes it on chain.

atoms.title: decentralized exchange (dex)
atoms.summary: A crypto venue where trades execute against a smart contract and assets stay in the trader's own custody throughout.

props.source_wording: Examples: Uniswap, SushiSwap, dYdX Self-custody throughout trading Permissionless, no KYC Higher fees (gas), potential MEV exposure Liquidity from liquidity pools
props.explanation: Nothing is deposited with an operator and nothing is gated by identity checks, which is what permissionless access means in practice. The costs are network fees on every interaction and exposure to having the trade front-run by whoever orders the block.

atoms.title: automated market maker (amm)
atoms.summary: A venue that prices trades from a formula over a pool of deposited reserves rather than by matching orders against a book.

props.source_wording: Bonding curve pricing (x * y = k constant product) No order book, trades against liquidity pool Price impact proportional to trade size Liquidity providers earn fees but face impermanent loss Examples: Uniswap V2/V3, Curve, Balancer
props.explanation: The pool always quotes, so there is no waiting for a counterparty, and the price walks along the curve as the reserves shift -- which is why size costs more here than in a book of comparable depth. Liquidity comes from depositors who earn the fees and carry [[Impermanent Loss]] against simply holding the two assets.

atoms.title: concentrated liquidity (clmm)
atoms.summary: An AMM design in which a provider supplies liquidity only across a chosen price range instead of the whole curve.

props.source_wording: Liquidity providers set price ranges More capital efficient than constant product AMMs Higher yields but requires active management Example: Uniswap V3
props.explanation: Capital sitting where price never trades earns nothing, so restricting the range multiplies the fees earned per unit deposited. The cost is that the position must be managed: once price leaves the range the position stops earning and is left entirely in one of the two assets.

atoms.title: constant product amm (uniswap v2)
atoms.summary: The invariant of a constant-product pool: the product of the two reserves is unchanged by a trade.

props.formula:
x * y = k

Output Amount = (y * Input Amount) / (x + Input Amount)
props.source_wording: The identity constant product amm (uniswap v2).
props.explanation: Holding the product constant is what defines the price at every point on the curve, and it is why the price moves against the trader as size grows -- the curve steepens as one reserve is drawn down. The output for a given input follows from the invariant alone.

atoms.title: price impact (amm)
atoms.summary: How far a trade moves the price of a constant-product pool, as a share of the reserve it trades against.

props.formula: Price Impact = Trade Size / (Pool Reserve + Trade Size)
props.source_wording: The quantity price impact (amm).
props.explanation: It follows from the size of the trade relative to the pool and from nothing else -- no queue, no counterparty, no time of day -- which makes execution cost on an AMM entirely predictable before the trade. It is a different quantity from the order-book [[Price Impact]] of chapter one, which measures how a book responds to order flow.

atoms.title: impermanent loss
atoms.summary: The shortfall of a liquidity position against simply holding the two assets, caused by the pool rebalancing as their relative price moves.

props.formula: IL = 2 * sqrt(price_ratio) / (1 + price_ratio) - 1
props.source_wording: The quantity impermanent loss.
props.explanation: The pool sells the asset that rises and buys the one that falls, so any divergence leaves the provider with less than the holder; it is called impermanent because it reverses if the price ratio returns. Fees are what has to cover it for provision to be worthwhile.

atoms.title: concentrated liquidity (v3)
atoms.summary: The real reserves a concentrated position must hold to provide a given depth over its chosen price range.

props.formula: Real Reserves = Virtual Reserves * (sqrt(P_upper) - sqrt(P_lower)) / sqrt(P_current)
props.source_wording: The quantity concentrated liquidity (v3).
props.explanation: Narrowing the range means the same depth is supplied by less capital, which is the whole gain of the design and the reason the position must be watched: outside the range it provides no depth at all.

atoms.title: fx basics
atoms.summary: The global market for exchanging currencies, the largest and most liquid market there is.

applications: Hedging foreign currency exposure for businesses
Carry trades exploiting interest rate differentials
Speculating on macroeconomic trends and central bank policy
Portfolio diversification across currencies
Arbitrage across currency crosses
examples: Quote Convention: EUR/USD = 1.0850 Interpretation: 1 Euro costs 1.0850 US Dollars Base currency: EUR Quote currency: USD
Pip Value Calculation: EUR/USD position: 100,000 units (1 standard lot) Pip = 0.0001 Pip Value = 100,000 * 0.0001 = $10 per pip
Carry Trade: Borrow JPY at 0.1% interest Invest in AUD at 4.0% interest Carry = 3.9% annually Risk: Currency movement can exceed carry return
Cross Rates: EUR/USD = 1.0850 USD/JPY = 150.00 EUR/JPY = 1.0850 * 150.00 = 162.75
props.source_wording: The foreign exchange (FX or forex) market is the global marketplace for trading currencies. It is the largest and most liquid financial market, with daily turnover exceeding $7 trillion, operating 24 hours from Sydney open to New York close.
props.explanation: It runs around the clock through overlapping regional sessions, with liquidity concentrated where they overlap, and prices are driven by the policy and rate expectations of the two central banks behind the pair. Its conventions -- pairs, pips, lots -- are what the arithmetic of a position rests on.

atoms.title: pip value
atoms.summary: What one pip of movement is worth in the quote currency, for a given lot size.

props.formula: Pip Value = (Pip Size / Exchange Rate) * Lot Size
props.source_wording: The quantity pip value.
props.explanation: It is what turns a rate move into money, and it depends on the pair and the lot rather than being a constant: sizing an FX position without it is sizing by rate rather than by risk.

atoms.title: position profit/loss
atoms.summary: The gain or loss on a position: the distance price travelled, valued at what one unit of movement is worth.

props.formula: P/L = (Exit Price - Entry Price) * Lot Size * Pip Value
props.source_wording: The quantity position profit/loss.
props.explanation: The two conventions in the chapter are the same arithmetic in different units -- FX values the move in pips times pip value, futures in ticks times [[Tick Value]] times contracts -- and both reduce to price distance times value per unit times size.

atoms.title: swap/rollover calculation
atoms.summary: The interest paid or received for holding an FX position overnight, from the rate differential between the two currencies.

props.formula: Swap = Position Size * (Base Currency Rate - Quote Currency Rate) / 365
props.source_wording: The quantity swap/rollover calculation.
props.explanation: It is the carry in a carry trade, applied nightly: long the higher-yielding currency earns it, and the reverse pays it. Over a long hold it can dominate the price move it was meant to accompany.

atoms.title: cross rate
atoms.summary: The rate between two currencies derived from each of their rates against a common third.

props.formula:
If EUR/USD = a and USD/JPY = b
Then EUR/JPY = a * b
props.source_wording: The quantity cross rate.
props.explanation: Most pairs are quoted against the dollar, so a rate between two others is implied by the two quotes; when the implied and quoted rates differ, the difference is a triangular arbitrage.

atoms.title: forward rate (interest rate parity)
atoms.summary: The exchange rate for a future date implied by the interest rates of the two currencies.

props.formula: F = S * ((1 + r_quote) / (1 + r_base))^T
props.source_wording: The quantity forward rate (interest rate parity).
props.explanation: Interest rate parity fixes it: the forward must offset the rate differential exactly, or borrowing in one currency and lending in the other would be riskless profit. It is also why a carry trade earns the differential only if the spot rate does not move to erase it.

atoms.title: settlement
atoms.summary: The transfer of securities and cash that completes a trade and moves ownership.

applications: Understanding when funds and securities become available
Managing cash flow around settlement dates
Assessing counterparty risk in OTC markets
Calculating margin requirements for cleared derivatives
Corporate action processing
props.source_wording: The process of transferring ownership of securities and funds between parties to complete a trade
props.explanation: A trade is an agreement; settlement is the moment it becomes ownership, and the delay between the two is what a settlement cycle names. Exchanging both legs simultaneously is what removes the risk of paying and receiving nothing.

atoms.title: clearing
atoms.summary: Validating and matching a trade after execution, and netting the obligations it creates, so that it is ready to settle.

props.source_wording: The process of validating, matching, and preparing trades for settlement, including netting of obligations
props.explanation: It is the step between agreeing a trade and exchanging value, and its main economy is netting: many gross obligations collapse into one net amount per party, so far less cash and stock needs to move. Where a [[Central Counterparty]] clears, it also guarantees the obligations it has netted.

atoms.title: central counterparty (ccp)
atoms.summary: An entity that steps between the two sides of a trade, becoming buyer to the seller and seller to the buyer so that neither depends on the other.

props.source_wording: Entity that interposes itself between buyers and sellers to guarantee trade completion
props.explanation: It converts a web of bilateral exposures into exposures to one guaranteed party, which is what makes anonymous trading and [[Netting]] possible at all. The guarantee is paid for with margin, and it concentrates the risk it removes -- the CCP is the party that must not fail.

atoms.title: equity settlement (t+2)
atoms.summary: Transfer of shares and cash two business days after an equity trade is executed.

props.source_wording: Trade executed Monday Settlement Wednesday Cash debited/credited and shares transferred
props.explanation: The gap between trade date and settlement date is why the cash for a purchase must be there later than the trade suggests, and why an entitlement such as a dividend depends on which date the holder is recorded on.

atoms.title: futures settlement (daily)
atoms.summary: Daily exchange of variation margin against the marked price, with a final settlement at expiration.

props.source_wording: Daily mark-to-market Variation margin exchanged each day Final settlement at expiration
props.explanation: A futures position is settled continuously rather than once: each day the gain or loss moves in cash, which is what keeps the exposure of the clearing house bounded. The final settlement is in cash or in delivery, depending on the contract.

atoms.title: crypto settlement
atoms.summary: Settlement of a crypto trade, either as an entry in an exchange ledger or as a confirmed transaction on a blockchain.

props.source_wording: CEX: Internal ledger, instant DEX: On-chain, block confirmation time (seconds to minutes) Withdrawal: Network confirmation required
props.explanation: The two are different in kind. On a centralized venue the trade settles instantly because nothing leaves the exchange; on chain, finality waits on block confirmation and costs a network fee. A withdrawal is where the internal ledger becomes an on-chain fact.

atoms.title: netting benefit
atoms.summary: How much of a set of gross obligations disappears once offsetting positions are netted.

props.formula:
Gross Obligations = Sum of all trade values
Net Obligation = |Total Buys - Total Sells|
Netting Efficiency = (Gross - Net) / Gross * 100%
props.source_wording: The quantity netting benefit.
props.explanation: It is the efficiency clearing exists to produce: the cash and stock that must actually move is the net, not the gross, and the ratio between them is what a clearing house is measured on.

atoms.title: exposure at default
atoms.summary: What would be owed if a counterparty failed now: the cost of replacing the position plus what it could still move against you.

props.formula: EAD = Replacement Cost + Potential Future Exposure
props.source_wording: The quantity exposure at default.
props.explanation: It is the number margin is sized against, and it is forward-looking on purpose -- the replacement cost at the moment of default is not the exposure, because the position must be reopened into whatever market caused the default.

atoms.title: contract specifications
atoms.summary: The standardised terms of a derivative contract -- size, tick increment, expiration and settlement method.

applications: Calculating position size and notional exposure
Determining margin requirements
Understanding roll procedures
Comparing similar contracts across exchanges
Backtesting with accurate contract specifications
examples: E-mini S&P 500 (ES): Exchange: CME Multiplier: $50 Tick Size: 0.25 points ($12.50) Settlement: Cash settled to S&P 500 index Expiration: Third Friday of contract month
Bitcoin Futures (BTC): Exchange: CME Multiplier: 5 BTC per contract Tick Size: $5 ($25 per tick) Settlement: Cash settled to CME CF Bitcoin Reference Rate
Crude Oil (CL): Exchange: NYMEX Multiplier: 1,000 barrels Tick Size: $0.01 ($10 per tick) Settlement: Physical delivery (most traders roll before expiration)
props.source_wording: Contract specifications define the standardized terms and conditions of derivative contracts, including size, tick increments, expiration rules, and settlement methods. Understanding specifications is essential for proper position sizing, risk calculation, and P&L computation.
props.explanation: The specification is what makes one contract fungible with another and is the arithmetic behind every position calculation: [[Notional Value]], [[Tick Value]] and margin all follow from the multiplier and the tick. Getting it wrong misstates exposure by whatever factor the multiplier is.

atoms.title: tick value
atoms.summary: What one minimum price increment is worth: tick size times the contract multiplier.

props.formula: Tick Value = Tick Size * Multiplier
props.source_wording: The quantity tick value.
props.explanation: It is the unit every futures profit and loss is counted in, and the reason two contracts on the same underlying can carry very different risk per point of index movement.

atoms.title: margin requirement (initial)
atoms.summary: The collateral needed to open a position, as a percentage of its notional value.

props.formula: Initial Margin = Notional Value * Initial Margin Percentage
props.source_wording: The quantity margin requirement (initial).
props.explanation: It is set by the venue rather than the trader and rises when volatility does, so the capital a position needs is not constant -- a requirement raised mid-position must be met from the same account that is already losing.

atoms.title: core principles
atoms.summary: Things that are true of this market whether or not anyone acts on them. A strategy does not get to disagree with one: it either accounts for it or pays for it.

atoms.title: best practices
atoms.summary: Things we follow because someone has already paid to learn them. Each is a default rather than a rule -- departing from one is often right, but it should be a decision with a reason.

atoms.title: the trend is your friend
atoms.summary: Trading with the prevailing trend is structurally safer than trading against it.

props.explanation: Trends persist longer than expected due to behavioral effects (herding, momentum ignition, institutional flows) Counter-trend trades have asymmetric risk: limited upside, potentially unlimited downside Mean reversion assumes prices will revert - but in strong trends, they often don't
props.caution: Do NOT describe mean reversion as "lower risk" or "safer" than trend following. Mean reversion has a high win rate but negative skew - losses, when they occur, are disproportionately large. Trend following has a low win rate but positive skew - you profit from letting winners run.

atoms.title: win rate is not risk
atoms.summary: A strategy's win rate tells you nothing about its risk profile without understanding skew.

props.explanation: Frequent small wins are psychologically rewarding This masks the tail risk of occasional large losses A single large loss can wipe out months of accumulated gains

atoms.title: risk is multi-dimensional
atoms.summary: Risk is not one number: per-trade exposure, the skew of the strategy, its fit to the regime, drawdown, tail losses and correlation are each a separate one.

comparison: Per-Trade Risk · Capital at risk on a single trade · Position size, stop loss
Strategy Skew · Distribution shape of outcomes · Positive (trend) vs. negative (MR)
Regime Risk · Mismatch between strategy and market · Mean reversion in a trending market
Drawdown Risk · Maximum capital decline · Max drawdown, recovery time
Tail Risk · Probability and magnitude of extreme losses · VaR, Expected Shortfall
Correlation Risk · Positions moving together in crisis · "Diversification" failing
props.caution: Critical: Reducing per-trade risk does NOT reduce strategy-level risk. A mean reversion strategy with tight stops still has negative skew.
props.source_wording: Risk cannot be reduced to a single number. Consider all dimensions:
props.explanation: They are independent, which is the part that gets missed -- tightening a stop lowers the first and leaves the second untouched. A mean reversion strategy with small losses still holds a large one, and positions that look diversified converge exactly when it matters.

atoms.title: regime determines archetype effectiveness
atoms.summary: Which family of strategy works is decided by the regime, not by the strategy.

comparison: Strong Trend · Trend following, Momentum · Mean reversion
Range-Bound · Mean reversion, Range trading · Trend following
High Volatility · Breakouts, Volatility strategies · Carry
Low Volatility · Carry, Mean reversion · Breakouts
props.caution: Identify the regime first, then select the archetype. Never apply a strategy blindly without regime context.
props.source_wording: Strategy archetypes rotate in effectiveness based on market regime.
props.explanation: Trend following and momentum earn in a strong trend and bleed in a range; mean reversion does the reverse. Breakouts need volatility and carry needs quiet. So the regime is read first and the archetype chosen second -- applying one without that read is a bet on the market being in the state the strategy happens to need.

atoms.title: candle body size
atoms.summary: The anatomy of one bar -- body, upper and lower wick, range, and the body as a share of the range.

props.formula:
Body = |Close - Open|
Upper Wick = High - max(Open, Close)
Lower Wick = min(Open, Close) - Low
Range = High - Low
Body Percentage = Body / Range * 100%
props.source_wording: The quantity candle body size.
props.explanation: It is what the reading of a single candle reduces to: a large body is agreement through the period, a long wick is a price the market visited and rejected.

atoms.title: swing point identification
atoms.summary: Marks a bar as a swing high or low when it exceeds the bars either side of it.

props.formula:
Swing High: High[i] > High[i-1] AND High[i] > High[i+1]
Swing Low: Low[i] < Low[i-1] AND Low[i] < Low[i+1]
props.source_wording: Computes swing point identification.
props.explanation: It is the primitive the rest of the chapter is built on: structure, liquidity pools and zones are all defined in terms of swings, so the lookback chosen here sets what everything downstream calls a trend.

atoms.title: fair value gaps
atoms.summary: A band of price that one impulsive move passed through without two-sided trade.

applications: Identifying pullback targets within trends
Finding entry points after impulsive moves
Setting realistic profit targets
Understanding where price might hesitate or reverse
Combining with supply/demand zones for higher confluence
examples: FVG as Entry: Uptrend established Impulsive move creates bullish FVG Wait for pullback into FVG Enter long when price touches upper portion of FVG Stop below FVG low Target previous high or higher timeframe resistance
props.source_wording: A Fair Value Gap (FVG), also called an imbalance, is a price range where significant price movement occurred with minimal trading on one side (gap between candle bodies). It represents an inefficiency in price delivery that the market often returns to fill or rebalance.
props.explanation: The market treats it as unfinished business and tends to return to it, which makes it a target for a pullback entry and a magnet for price that has run too far. A gap that is filled has done its work; an unfilled one is still pulling.

atoms.title: bullish fair value gap
atoms.summary: A three-candle imbalance where the third candle's low stays above the first candle's high, leaving a band price rose through without trading.

props.source_wording: Candle 1: Any candle Candle 2: Large bullish candle (impulse) Candle 3: Candle 3's low is above Candle 1's high FVG Zone: From Candle 1's high to Candle 3's low Expectation: Price may pull back into this zone before continuing up
props.explanation: It marks delivery too fast to be two-sided, and the market tends to return and trade the band before continuing up. The band runs from the first high to the third low.

atoms.title: bearish fair value gap
atoms.summary: A three-candle imbalance where the third candle's high stays below the first candle's low, leaving a band price fell through without trading.

props.source_wording: Candle 1: Any candle Candle 2: Large bearish candle (impulse) Candle 3: Candle 3's high is below Candle 1's low FVG Zone: From Candle 1's low to Candle 3's high Expectation: Price may pull back into this zone before continuing down
props.explanation: The gap is where selling was so one-sided that no two-way trade happened, and price often returns to it before continuing down. The band runs from the first low to the third high.

atoms.title: bullish fvg detection
atoms.summary: Detects a bullish gap: the third candle's low above the first candle's high.

props.formula:
Bullish_FVG = Low[candle_3] > High[candle_1]
FVG_Top = Low[candle_3]
FVG_Bottom = High[candle_1]
FVG_Size = FVG_Top - FVG_Bottom
props.source_wording: Computes bullish fvg detection.
props.explanation: Three candles are enough because the imbalance is defined by the outer two failing to overlap -- the middle candle is the impulse that caused it.

atoms.title: bearish fvg detection
atoms.summary: Detects a bearish gap: the third candle's high below the first candle's low.

props.formula:
Bearish_FVG = High[candle_3] < Low[candle_1]
FVG_Top = Low[candle_1]
FVG_Bottom = High[candle_3]
FVG_Size = FVG_Top - FVG_Bottom
props.source_wording: Computes bearish fvg detection.
props.explanation: The two bounding prices become the zone, and its size is what the significance filter is applied to.

atoms.title: fvg validity (significance filter)
atoms.summary: Keeps only gaps larger than half the [[Average True Range]].

props.formula: Valid_FVG = FVG_Size > ATR * 0.5
props.source_wording: Computes fvg validity (significance filter).
props.explanation: Every noisy series produces small gaps constantly; without a size filter the chart fills with them and none of them mean anything.

atoms.title: fvg fill status
atoms.summary: Classifies a gap as unfilled, partially filled or filled by how far price has traded back through it.

props.formula:
Filled = Price has traded through entire FVG zone
Partially_Filled = Price entered zone but didn't fully traverse
Unfilled = Price hasn't touched zone
props.source_wording: Computes fvg fill status.
props.explanation: The status is what makes a gap tradeable or spent: an unfilled gap is still a target, and a filled one is history.

atoms.title: volume profile
atoms.summary: The distribution of traded volume across price rather than across time.

props.volume_profile_interpretation: **Point of Control (POC):** - Represents the "fairest price" where most business occurred - Acts as a magnet drawing price back to it - Better suited as trade completion zone than trade initiation zone - Multiple days with similar POC indicate strong fair value acceptance **Value Area:** - Contains ~70% of session volume - VAH and VAL act as support/resistance levels - Opening inside prior VA suggests balanced, rotational day - Opening outside prior VA suggests directional move likely
props.auction_market_scenario: **Opening Inside Previous Value Area:** Expectation: Balanced, two-sided trade Behavior: Price likely to rotate between VAH and VAL Strategy: Mean reversion, fade extremes **Opening Above Previous VAH:** Expectation: Bullish continuation or fade opportunity If value migrates higher: Buyers in control, trend continuation If value stays in prior range: Gap fill likely, sellers absorbing **Opening Below Previous VAL:** Expectation: Bearish continuation or fade opportunity If value migrates lower: Sellers in control, trend continuation If value stays in prior range: Gap fill likely, buyers absorbing
props.value_migration_analysis: def analyze_value_migration(today_va, yesterday_va): """ Determine if buyers or sellers made progress """ if today_va['vah'] > yesterday_va['vah'] and today_va['val'] > yesterday_va['val']: return 'BUYERS_PROGRESSING' elif today_va['vah'] < yesterday_va['vah'] and today_va['val'] < yesterday_va['val']: return 'SELLERS_PROGRESSING' elif today_va['vah'] > yesterday_va['vah'] and today_va['val'] < yesterday_va['val']: return 'RANGE_EXPANSION' else: return 'OVERLAPPING_BALANCE'
props.using_poc_and_va_for_trading: **POC as Target:** - Mean reversion trades often target POC - Price tends to revisit POC during balanced sessions - Multiple touches of POC increase its significance **VAH/VAL as Entry Zones:** - Enter long near VAL in uptrend with stop below - Enter short near VAH in downtrend with stop above - Failed breaks of VA boundaries signal reversals **Developing vs. Naked POC:** - Current session POC: May shift as session develops - Prior session POC: Static reference level (naked if untested) - Naked POCs act as magnets and often get tested
props.source_wording: Volume Profile displays trading activity distributed across price levels rather than time, revealing where the most trading occurred. Market Auction Theory views markets as continuous auctions where price seeks fair value through the interaction of buyers and sellers. Together, these concepts identify where institutions trade and where price is likely to react.
props.explanation: It answers a different question from a chart of price over time: not where price went, but where business was actually done. From it come the [[Point of Control]] and the value area, and with them the auction reading of a market -- price advertises, volume accepts or rejects, and value migrates when one side keeps making progress.

atoms.title: point of control
atoms.summary: The price with the most volume traded in a session -- where the most business was done.

props.source_wording: POC. Price level with highest traded volume in the session
props.explanation: It is the session's fairest price by the market's own vote, and price returns to it during balanced trade, which makes it a better target than an entry.

atoms.title: value area high
atoms.summary: The upper edge of the range holding roughly seventy per cent of a session's volume.

props.source_wording: VAH. Upper boundary of the value area (70% of volume)
props.explanation: It is the boundary between accepted value and price the market has rejected, so a session opening above it is making a directional statement rather than rotating.

atoms.title: value area low
atoms.summary: The lower edge of the range holding roughly seventy per cent of a session's volume.

props.source_wording: VAL. Lower boundary of the value area
props.explanation: Together with [[Value Area High]] it bounds where business was done, and both act as levels in the next session for the same reason a [[High Volume Node]] does.

atoms.title: high volume node
atoms.summary: A price level where a lot of volume has traded.

props.source_wording: HVN. Price level with significant volume accumulation
props.explanation: Business done at a price is agreement about value, and price tends to slow there, which is why these act as support and resistance without being drawn from swings.

atoms.title: low volume node
atoms.summary: A price level where little volume has traded.

props.source_wording: LVN. Price level with minimal volume (often acts as magnet)
props.explanation: Little business means little agreement, so price crosses these quickly rather than settling in them -- which makes them poor targets and good places to expect acceleration.

atoms.title: value area calculation
atoms.summary: Grows a range outward from the [[Point of Control]], taking the busier side each step, until it holds seventy per cent of the volume.

props.formula:
1. Identify POC (highest volume price)
2. Add volume from one tick above and one tick below POC
3. Continue adding volume from side with greater volume
4. Stop when cumulative volume reaches 70% of total
5. Upper bound = VAH, Lower bound = VAL
props.source_wording: Computes value area calculation.
props.explanation: Building outward from the busiest price is what makes the area an observation about where business was done rather than a standard deviation of a distribution nobody checked was normal.

atoms.title: volume profile metrics
atoms.summary: The width of the value area, in price and as a share of the session range.

props.formula:
Value Area Range = VAH - VAL
VA Percentage of Range = (VAH - VAL) / (Session High - Session Low) * 100

Interpretation:
- Tight VA (< 40% of range): Strong directional day
- Wide VA (> 70% of range): Balanced, rotational day
props.source_wording: The quantity volume profile metrics.
props.explanation: A narrow value area against a wide session says the market spent its time in one place and travelled through the rest -- a directional day. A wide one says it rotated.

atoms.title: market structure
atoms.summary: The arrangement of swing highs and lows that says whether a market is trending or ranging.

applications: Determining trend direction objectively
Identifying trend continuation vs. reversal points
Setting stop-loss levels based on structural invalidation
Finding high-probability entry points after structural breaks
Aligning trades with higher timeframe structure
examples:
Uptrend Structure: Each high exceeds previous high Each low exceeds previous low Long bias maintained until CHoCH HH3
   /
 HH2   
 /  \
HH1  HL3
/  \  /
HL1 HL2
Break of Structure (BOS) - Bullish: Uptrend established with HH/HL sequence Price pulls back creating new HL Price breaks above most recent HH Confirmation of trend continuation
Change of Character (CHoCH) - Bearish: Uptrend with HH/HL sequence Price fails to make new HH (creates LH) Price breaks below most recent HL First signal of potential trend reversal
props.source_wording: Market structure refers to the arrangement of price highs and lows that define the current state and direction of a market. It provides a framework for understanding whether a market is trending (up or down) or ranging, and identifies key structural shifts that signal potential reversals.
props.explanation: It gives trend a definition that can be checked rather than eyeballed: higher highs with higher lows, or lower lows with lower highs, and neither in a range. Because it is defined by swings it repeats at every timeframe, and it supplies the level at which a position is wrong -- the structural point whose break invalidates the read.

atoms.title: break of structure (bos)
atoms.summary: Price closing beyond the most recent swing point in the direction of the trend.

props.explanation: It is the continuation signal: the sequence of higher highs and higher lows extends rather than fails, which is what distinguishes it from a [[Change of Character]]. It is also where the invalidation level for the position moves to.

atoms.title: change of character (choch)
atoms.summary: Price breaking structure against the prevailing trend -- the first break that does not fit the sequence.

props.source_wording: Reversal signal where price breaks structure against the prevailing trend
props.explanation: It is a warning rather than a reversal: the trend has stopped extending, which is not yet the same as turning. Treating it as an entry rather than as notice to tighten is the mistake the chapter warns about.

atoms.title: trend classification
atoms.summary: Classifies the market as up, down or ranging by comparing consecutive swing highs and lows.

props.formula:
Uptrend: Swing_High[n] > Swing_High[n-1] AND Swing_Low[n] > Swing_Low[n-1]
Downtrend: Swing_High[n] < Swing_High[n-1] AND Swing_Low[n] < Swing_Low[n-1]
Range: Neither condition met
props.source_wording: Computes trend classification.
props.explanation: It turns "the trend is up" into something two people can check and agree on, and it returns a range whenever the two conditions disagree rather than guessing.

atoms.title: structure break detection
atoms.summary: Marks a break of structure when a close passes the previous swing high or low.

props.formula:
BOS_Bullish: Close > Previous_Swing_High
BOS_Bearish: Close < Previous_Swing_Low
props.source_wording: Computes structure break detection.
props.explanation: On the close rather than on the wick, which is what separates a structural break from a sweep of the same level.

atoms.title: trending market
atoms.summary: A market making higher highs and higher lows, or lower lows and lower highs, with pullbacks shallow against the moves that make them.

props.source_wording: Clear higher highs/higher lows (uptrend) or lower highs/lower lows (downtrend) Moving averages fanning out and sloping in trend direction Pullbacks are shallow relative to impulse moves ADX above 25 indicating trend strength Best strategy: Trend following, momentum
props.explanation: Moving averages separate and slope, and [[ADX]] holds above twenty-five. This is where trend following and momentum work and where mean reversion is most dangerous, because the reversion it waits for does not come.

atoms.title: ranging market
atoms.summary: A market oscillating between a floor and a ceiling, making no directional progress.

props.source_wording: Price oscillating between support and resistance Moving averages flat and intertwined Higher highs followed by lower lows (no consistency) ADX below 20 indicating lack of trend Best strategy: Mean reversion, range trading
props.explanation: Moving averages flatten and cross, and [[ADX]] sits below twenty. Mean reversion is what works here and trend following is what bleeds, which is the whole reason to classify the state before choosing the strategy.

atoms.title: compression
atoms.summary: A phase of contracting range and falling volatility.

props.source_wording: Decreasing range (ATR declining) Bollinger Bands squeezing Triangles, wedges, or rectangles forming Decreasing volume Preparation for breakout
props.explanation: Ranges narrow, bands squeeze and volume dries up while the market waits. It resolves into [[Expansion]], which is why compression is read as a setup rather than as a state to trade inside.

atoms.title: expansion
atoms.summary: A phase of widening range and rising volatility.

props.source_wording: Increasing range (ATR rising) Bollinger Bands expanding Strong directional candles Increasing volume Trend initiation or continuation
props.explanation: Directional candles, rising [[Average True Range]] and rising volume: this is where trends begin and resume, and where a strategy fitted to the quiet phase before it stops working.

atoms.title: adx trend strength
atoms.summary: Classifies the market as trending, ranging or transitional from the level of [[ADX]].

props.formula:
ADX > 25: Trending market
ADX < 20: Ranging market
ADX 20-25: Transitional
props.source_wording: Computes adx trend strength.
props.explanation: Above twenty-five is a trend, below twenty is a range, and between them is the state in which most strategies are least reliable. It measures how strong a trend is and says nothing about which way it points.

atoms.title: bollinger band width (compression measure)
atoms.summary: The distance between the bands as a fraction of the middle band.

props.formula: BB Width = (Upper Band - Lower Band) / Middle Band
props.source_wording: The quantity bollinger band width (compression measure).
props.explanation: It is the standard measure of a squeeze: low and falling is compression, rising is the expansion that follows it.

atoms.title: atr percentage
atoms.summary: The [[Average True Range]] as a percentage of price.

props.formula: ATR% = ATR / Close * 100
props.source_wording: The quantity atr percentage.
props.explanation: Expressing range against price is what makes two instruments comparable, and its direction is the objective form of [[Compression]] and [[Expansion]].

atoms.title: range ratio
atoms.summary: The current range against the average range of recent periods.

props.formula: Range Ratio = Current Range / Average Range (n periods)
props.source_wording: The quantity range ratio.
props.explanation: Below half is compression and above one and a half is expansion, which turns the phase of the volatility cycle into a number rather than an impression.

atoms.title: liquidity pools
atoms.summary: A cluster of resting orders -- stops and pending entries -- at a level everyone can see.

props.source_wording: Clusters of stop-loss orders and pending orders at predictable levels
props.explanation: Price is drawn towards them because that is where size can be filled, which inverts the naive reading of a level: the obvious stop is not protection but a target.

atoms.title: stop hunts
atoms.summary: A move that runs the stops clustered at an obvious level and then turns.

props.source_wording: Price moves designed to trigger clustered stops before reversing
props.explanation: It is [[Liquidity Grab]] seen from the side of the trader who was stopped out, and it is the argument for placing stops past the obvious level rather than on it.

atoms.title: liquidity grab
atoms.summary: A quick move into a pool of resting orders followed immediately by a reversal.

props.source_wording: Quick move to liquidity zone followed by reversal
props.explanation: It is how a large order gets filled without paying for the whole move: the stops it triggers supply the other side. Read as a breakout it is a loss; read as a sweep it is the entry.

atoms.title: smart money concept
atoms.summary: The reading of price as the footprint of participants large enough to need other people's orders to fill their own.

props.source_wording: Institutional traders need liquidity to fill large orders
props.explanation: The claim is mechanical rather than conspiratorial: size cannot be filled where there is no liquidity, so it is filled where the stops are. Whether the label is right, the constraint it names is real.

atoms.title: equal highs and lows
atoms.summary: Two or more touches at the same level, which is where stops collect.

props.source_wording: Multiple touches at same price create "equal highs" or "equal lows" Represent obvious stop-loss locations (retail traders place stops there) High probability of being swept before a real move
props.explanation: The obviousness is what makes them liquidity: every trader who drew the same line put a stop just beyond it. The chapter's advice follows from that -- expect the level to be swept before any real move, and place stops past it rather than at it.

atoms.title: buy-side liquidity
atoms.summary: Resting buy orders above the market -- the stops of short positions and the entry orders of breakout buyers.

props.source_wording: Location: Above recent swing highs, above equal highs Contents: Stop-losses from short positions, buy stop orders Action: Price sweeps above, triggers stops, then reverses down
props.explanation: It sits where everyone can see it: above swing highs and above [[Equal Highs and Lows]]. That visibility is the point, because a large seller needs buyers to sell into, and this is where they are.

atoms.title: sell-side liquidity
atoms.summary: Resting sell orders below the market -- the stops of long positions and the entry orders of breakdown sellers.

props.source_wording: Location: Below recent swing lows, below equal lows Contents: Stop-losses from long positions, sell stop orders Action: Price sweeps below, triggers stops, then reverses up
props.explanation: It gathers under swing lows and under [[Equal Highs and Lows]], and it is where a large buyer finds the size to buy.

atoms.title: liquidity zone identification
atoms.summary: Places the buy-side and sell-side pools a fraction of an [[Average True Range]] beyond the recent swing high and low.

props.formula:
Buy-Side Liquidity = Swing_High + ATR_Buffer
Sell-Side Liquidity = Swing_Low - ATR_Buffer

Where ATR_Buffer = ATR * 0.5 to 1.0
props.source_wording: Computes liquidity zone identification.
props.explanation: The buffer is the point: stops sit past the level rather than on it, so the zone that gets swept is above the high rather than at it.

atoms.title: equal level detection
atoms.summary: Finds highs or lows matching within a tolerance -- the levels where stops gather.

props.formula:
Equal Highs: |High[i] - High[j]| < Threshold AND i != j
Equal Lows: |Low[i] - Low[j]| < Threshold AND i != j
props.source_wording: Computes equal level detection.
props.explanation: The tolerance is what makes it usable: exact equality almost never occurs, and a level a few ticks apart is the same level to everyone looking at it.

atoms.title: volume
atoms.summary: How much traded in a period -- the amount of activity behind a price move.

applications: Confirming breakouts and trend moves
Identifying accumulation and distribution phases
Spotting divergences between price and volume
Detecting institutional activity
Timing entries and exits based on volume patterns
props.source_wording: Volume represents the number of shares, contracts, or units traded during a specific period. Order flow analysis studies the sequence and characteristics of executed trades to understand the balance between buying and selling pressure and identify institutional activity.
props.explanation: It is the second dimension of every move: the same distance travelled on twice the volume is a different event, because more participants had to agree to produce it. Comparing effort against result is what separates a move that will hold from one that will not.

atoms.title: volume confirmation
atoms.summary: The requirement that a breakout come with above-average volume before it is believed.

props.source_wording: Breakout above resistance on 2x average volume = Confirmed Breakout above resistance on below-average volume = Suspect, likely to fail
props.explanation: A move on thin volume is a move few people took part in, and those are the breakouts that fail back into the range. Requiring it costs some genuine breakouts and avoids most false ones.

atoms.title: volume divergence
atoms.summary: Price making new extremes while volume does not follow.

props.source_wording: Price making higher highs Volume making lower highs Warning: Momentum weakening, potential reversal
props.explanation: Participation is draining out of the move even as it continues, which is a warning rather than a signal: divergences persist far longer than they look like they should.

atoms.title: accumulation pattern
atoms.summary: Sideways price with volume weighted towards up days -- the footprint of a buyer working a large order without moving the price.

examples: Indication: Smart money accumulating
props.source_wording: Price trading sideways Volume higher on up days than down days On-Balance Volume rising while price flat
props.explanation: The tell is effort without result in one direction only: [[On-Balance Volume]] rises while price stays flat. It is read as a large participant building a position quietly, and it ends when the range breaks upward.

atoms.title: distribution pattern
atoms.summary: Sideways price with volume weighted towards down days -- a large seller working out of a position near the highs.

examples: Indication: Smart money distributing
props.source_wording: Price trading sideways near highs Volume higher on down days than up days On-Balance Volume falling while price flat
props.explanation: It is the mirror of [[Accumulation Pattern]]: [[On-Balance Volume]] falls while price holds up, and the range usually breaks down. Price alone shows nothing, which is the reason to look at volume at all.

atoms.title: climactic volume
atoms.summary: A volume spike several times normal at a price extreme.

props.source_wording: Volume spike 3x+ normal levels Often at market extremes (tops/bottoms) Can signal exhaustion and reversal
props.explanation: It reads as exhaustion rather than confirmation: everyone who was going to act has acted, and there is no one left to continue the move. The same magnitude in the middle of a range means nothing of the kind.

atoms.title: relative volume
atoms.summary: Current volume against the average for the same period.

props.formula: RVOL = Current_Volume / Average_Volume(n periods)
props.source_wording: The quantity relative volume.
props.explanation: Absolute volume says nothing without its own baseline: above one and a half is real participation, and it is the objective form of the confirmation the chapter demands of a breakout.

atoms.title: delta (order flow)
atoms.summary: Buy volume minus sell volume, and its running total.

props.formula:
Delta = Buy_Volume - Sell_Volume
Cumulative Delta = Running sum of Delta
props.source_wording: The quantity delta (order flow).
props.explanation: Volume says how much traded; delta says which side was the aggressor. A rising price on negative cumulative delta is a move being sold into, which is invisible in volume alone.

atoms.title: volume profile
atoms.summary: Sums traded volume at each price level and takes the busiest as the point of control.

props.formula:
For each price level:
  Volume_at_Price[P] = Sum of volume traded at price P
Point of Control (POC) = Price with highest Volume_at_Price
props.source_wording: Computes volume profile.
props.explanation: This is the computation behind the profile: bin by price rather than by time, and the shape that results is where the levels come from.

atoms.title: support and resistance
atoms.summary: Price levels where buying or selling has repeatedly been strong enough to stop a move.

applications: Identifying entry points near support in uptrends
Identifying exit points near resistance
Setting stop-loss levels below support or above resistance
Planning breakout trades above resistance or below support
Mapping key levels for position management
examples: Role Reversal Example: Price approaches resistance at $50 Multiple rejections from $50 (confirmed resistance) Price eventually breaks above $50 Price pulls back to $50 $50 now acts as support (role reversal) Price bounces from $50 and continues higher
props.source_wording: Support is a price level where buying pressure is expected to overcome selling pressure, causing a decline to pause or reverse. Resistance is a price level where selling pressure is expected to overcome buying pressure, causing an advance to pause or reverse.
props.explanation: They work because participants remember them and act again at the same price, which is why a broken level reverses role: the buyers defending it become the sellers trapped above it. They are zones rather than lines, and their weight comes from the timeframe they were drawn on and how strongly price reacted before.

atoms.title: horizontal level
atoms.summary: A support or resistance level fixed at a price -- a prior swing, a level tested repeatedly, a round number, a high-volume node.

examples: Previous swing highs/lows Multiple price touches at same level Round numbers ($100, $50, etc.) High-volume nodes from volume profile
props.explanation: It holds because enough participants remember the same price, which is also why it stops holding once everyone has traded around it.

atoms.title: dynamic level
atoms.summary: A support or resistance level that moves with price: a moving average, a trend line, VWAP, a band.

props.source_wording: Moving averages (20 EMA, 50 SMA, 200 SMA) Trend lines connecting highs or lows Indicator levels (VWAP, Bollinger Bands)
props.explanation: It is the same idea as a horizontal level with a different anchor -- the level is computed from recent price rather than fixed at one -- and it is why the same instrument can respect a rising line it never touched at a fixed price.

atoms.title: support/resistance zone width
atoms.summary: How wide to draw a level, scaled to the [[Average True Range]].

props.formula:
Zone Width = ATR * 0.5 to 1.0
Support Zone = Level - Zone_Width to Level + Zone_Width/2
Resistance Zone = Level - Zone_Width/2 to Level + Zone_Width
props.source_wording: The quantity support/resistance zone width.
props.explanation: Drawing a zone rather than a line is what accommodates the wicks that pierce every level; scaling it to volatility is what keeps one instrument's zone from being another's noise.

atoms.title: level strength score
atoms.summary: How much weight a level carries, from the number of touches, the timeframes it appears on and the volume traded there.

props.formula: Strength = Number_of_Touches + (Timeframe_Weight * Timeframe_Count) + Volume_Weight
props.source_wording: The quantity level strength score.
props.explanation: It makes explicit what is usually a judgement call, so that two levels can be ranked instead of both being drawn and treated alike.

atoms.title: pivot points (classic)
atoms.summary: A level derived from the previous period's high, low and close, with supports and resistances stepped out from it.

props.formula:
Pivot = (High + Low + Close) / 3
R1 = (2 * Pivot) - Low
S1 = (2 * Pivot) - High
R2 = Pivot + (High - Low)
S2 = Pivot - (High - Low)
props.source_wording: The quantity pivot points (classic).
props.explanation: The value is not in the arithmetic but in how many participants compute the same numbers from the same bar, which is what makes them levels at all.

atoms.title: supply & demand zones
atoms.summary: The area a strong impulsive move began from, expected to matter again when price returns.

applications: Identifying high-probability reversal areas
Finding entries with excellent risk/reward ratios
Understanding institutional order flow
Setting precise stop-loss levels
Planning trades around pending zone tests
examples: Zone Quality Factors: Strength of departure: Stronger moves indicate stronger zones Time at zone: Shorter basing periods suggest more urgent imbalance Freshness: First touch of zone is highest probability Trend alignment: Zones in trend direction are more reliable
props.source_wording: Supply and demand zones are price areas where significant imbalances between buyers and sellers caused strong price moves. Unlike traditional support/resistance, these zones focus on the origin of moves and expect price to react when returning to these areas.
props.explanation: It is defined by the origin of a move rather than by how often a level has been touched, which is what distinguishes it from [[Support and Resistance]]. Fresh zones are the claim; a zone tested twice has spent whatever imbalance it held.

atoms.title: demand zone
atoms.summary: The base a strong rally departed from, taken to hold buying that was never filled.

props.source_wording: Price trading sideways or declining (base formation) Strong bullish candle(s) break up from the base The base area becomes a demand zone When price returns to zone, expect buying response Zone extends from base low to base high
props.explanation: The claim is about the origin of the move rather than the number of touches, which is what separates it from [[Support and Resistance]]. It is strongest untested, and it weakens each time price returns to it.

atoms.title: supply zone
atoms.summary: The base a strong decline departed from, taken to hold selling that was never filled.

props.source_wording: Price trading sideways or rising (base formation) Strong bearish candle(s) break down from the base The base area becomes a supply zone When price returns to zone, expect selling response Zone extends from base low to base high
props.explanation: The mirror of [[Demand Zone]]: the stronger and faster the move away, the stronger the claim that unfilled orders remain behind it.

atoms.title: zone identification
atoms.summary: Marks the consolidation before an impulsive move as a zone, valid when the departure exceeds twice the [[Average True Range]].

props.formula:
Demand Zone:
  - Base_Low = Lowest low in consolidation before bullish breakout
  - Base_High = Highest candle body before breakout candle
  - Valid if: Breakout_Move > 2 * ATR

Supply Zone:
